scope: 02_rules.md:Answered question OQ-17 — Dependency vulnerability and update policy

topics.topic: Definition, cutoff, completeness, and consistency of the single OSV copy used per deploy
questions: What makes the OSV data one coherent copy, and at what instant is an advisory considered to have been added, changed, or withdrawn after the read?

For a paged, streamed, mirrored, or per-package OSV read, what establishes the single cutoff instant and proves that a syntactically readable copy is complete rather than partial, so the deploy can pass?
Must the check use an immutable complete OSV snapshot with one revision identity, or may it issue package queries during one check, and how is a partial or changing result detected?

quotes:
Before it,
every distribution installed in that image — the pins and every library
pip resolves for them — is checked against the OSV database (osv.dev,
ecosystem PyPI; it aggregates the PyPA advisory database), read once in
that same deploy as one copy of the PyPI ecosystem data, against which
every distribution is judged; no earlier verdict or advisory copy is
reused.

Each deploy makes one check, and its
verdict on the one copy it read decides that deploy; an advisory added,
changed or withdrawn after that read is judged by the next deploy.

DEP-002: the deploy step judges every distribution installed in the
built image, bound to that image's content id, against the one copy of OSV
data read in the same deploy, and starts the service only on a passing verdict about
that same image; a listed version, unreadable or unmatchable advisory
data, a verdict from an earlier deploy, or a verdict about another image
does not start it
[witness: verification:dependency_release_gate_client_portal].
judgement.divergence: One implementation fixes a coherent OSV cutoff before acquisition and defers every later advisory change; another uses sequential live responses and may include only changes visible to later requests, so the deployment operator sees the same image start or remain stopped.
judgement.why: The texts require one copy and one read but do not define the consistency boundary or completeness condition needed to decide which advisory state governs a deploy.

witness.initial: A built image contains distributions A and B, and obtaining OSV data requires multiple responses.
events: The deployment process begins its one OSV check.
OSV adds an advisory affecting both distributions after A's response but before B's response.
The check completes and decides whether to start the service.
outcomes: The copy is cut off before acquisition, so neither distribution is blocked until the next deploy and the service starts.
The sequential responses form the copy, so B is judged with the new advisory and the service does not start.
basis: A deploy is the start of the service from a built image.

Each deploy makes one check, and its
verdict on the one copy it read decides that deploy; an advisory added,
changed or withdrawn after that read is judged by the next deploy.

questions: Which existing witness check is bound to CLK-002 and will assert its source restriction, wall-clock read counts, audit-writer exception, elapsed-clock confinement, and viewer-entry boundary behavior?

Which existing witness check is bound to the CLK-002 Required tests and asserts the clock-source exclusivity, exact wall-read counts, audit-writer counts, expiry boundary, and viewer-entry elapsed-read boundary?
Which existing check is bound to CLK-002 and will assert its clock-reader, reading-count, reuse, and elapsed-clock obligations?

judgement.why: This is the same question as P1 about the absence of an existing witness binding for CLK-002, and the relevant witness line has not changed.

precedent.why: The exhaustive witness line binds both existing checks to CLK-001 and therefore answers that no existing witness check is bound to CLK-002.

topics.topic: Accepted source-supplied datetime representations and normalization to offset-naive UTC
questions: When a permitted source representation is offset-aware or has a non-UTC offset, must the test expect literal representation preservation or conversion to the equivalent offset-naive UTC value?
Which input representations are accepted for source-supplied datetimes, especially offset-naive values, and how is each accepted value converted to offset-naive UTC without changing its instant?

judgement.why: This is the same question as P8 about accepted datetime representations and normalization to offset-naive UTC, and the relevant clock-policy passage has not changed.

precedent.topic: Accepted datetime inputs and timestamp normalization semantics
quotes:
Times a
source supplies — `approved_at`, `published_at` of a snapshot, `confirmed_at`
of a recognition, `photo_date`, a service credential's `expires_at` — are
kept as supplied: the same instant, stored offset-naive UTC like every
persisted timestamp, never replaced by the clock (State 1 Modeling
conventions). Calendar dates a source supplies — `document_date` of a
recognition, `payment_date` — are `date` values, kept as the supplied
calendar day: they carry no time or offset, are never converted to an
instant and never replaced by the clock's day; their accepted forms and checks, and where in an operation
its one clock read happens, are the accepted spec's, carried to States 6–7.
precedent.why: The passage already makes “stored as supplied” preserve the instant while normalizing storage to offset-naive UTC, while the accepted wire representations and validation checks are formats and field-type contracts owned by State 6.

topics.topic: OSV package/version matching rules and fail-closed handling of parsing or matching uncertainty
questions: How are an installed distribution and version matched to an OSV PyPI package and affected-version expression, and which matching uncertainties fail the whole deploy?
Which OSV parsing or matching failures make the whole deploy check incomplete, including failures in entries unrelated to an installed distribution?

quotes:
A distribution has a known vulnerability when an OSV entry that is not
withdrawn lists its installed version as affected; reachability inside
the portal is not judged case by case, so such a distribution blocks the
deploy whatever feature the advisory concerns.

complete does not pass: that deploy does not start the service, and a

judgement.divergence: One implementation applies canonical PyPI name and version-range matching and blocks a matching installed distribution; another uses literal names or treats an unrelated malformed entry as ignorable, so the deployment operator sees the service remain stopped or start.
judgement.why: Neither package/version matching nor the scope of parsing failures that make the whole check incomplete is defined, although both determine the deploy refusal.

topics.topic: Receiving state, required decisions, and named check for the deployment-procedure handoff
questions: Which receiving state owns that deployment procedure, what decided execution must it implement to acquire the one OSV copy and bind the verdict to the exact image, and what check confirms the handoff rather than leaving the tool choice open as ‘later’?

Which later state receives the deployment-procedure obligation, and what named check confirms that its still-open choices—OSV acquisition, package/version matching, failure classification, and image binding—were decided there?

quotes:
The tool that runs the
check is a deployment procedure, not a portal rule, carried to the
deploy route.

No value enters the specification (SPEC_STANDARD 15.3.1: no path to generated
code); the decision is operational and owned by the Factory deployment route.
judgement.why: The concrete deployment procedure and its implementation notes belong to State 7, while State 2 already names the required release-gate witness.

topics.topic: Verification that no unauthorized direct or indirect host-clock APIs are used
questions: How must the Required tests detect other ways of reading a host clock, such as `os.clock_gettime`, an event-loop clock, or a third-party clock API?
How must the required check demonstrate that no other host-clock API or indirect wrapper reads wall or elapsed time?

quotes:
CLK-002: the clock source is the only reader of the host's wall and
elapsed clocks; an operation takes one wall reading, and that instant
decides every current-time comparison it makes and every portal-owned
timestamp it writes (the audit writer's reading of `occurred_at` aside);

CLK-002: a source check that no module other than the clock source
imports the `time` module or calls `now`, `utcnow` or `today` of
`datetime` or `date`, under any name, and that only the A25 viewer-entry
rate limiter calls the elapsed reading, passing its value to no store,
no audit and no `datetime` or `timedelta`; a test per operation that
reads the wall clock, with a counting wall-clock source, that the
operation takes exactly one wall reading and the audit writer one per
appended record, and that an expiry equal to that reading is refused
while the timestamps it writes equal that reading; and a viewer-entry
test with a counting clock source that one request takes exactly one
elapsed reading and that the window decision at its boundary follows
that reading.
judgement.divergence: One verifier checks only the enumerated imports and calls and accepts a non-clock module using `os.clock_gettime`; another verifies all direct and indirect host-clock access and rejects it, while a staff caller can observe different expiry decisions.
judgement.why: The Required test enumerates only some host-clock APIs and does not say how clock-reader exclusivity is established for other primitives or wrappers.

service principal, its authenticated bearer credential of R0-09, which needs
no separate session), active principal, access to the concrete `project_id`,
required capability, and Registry project lifecycle policy (R0-15).

session, credential or token is usable while `now < expires_at` and expired
from `now = expires_at` on (Factory code `application/authorization_guard.py`,
`application/service_identity.py`).

topics.topic: Whether withdrawn OSV advisories still block deployment
questions: When the only OSV entry listing the installed version as affected is withdrawn, must the deploy start or be refused?
Does a withdrawn OSV entry that still lists the installed version as affected block deployment?

judgement.why: This is the same question as P5 about withdrawn OSV entries, and the defining normative passage has not changed.

precedent.topic: Whether withdrawn affected-version OSV entries block deployment
quotes:
A distribution has a known vulnerability when an OSV entry that is not
   withdrawn lists its installed version as affected; reachability inside
   the portal is not judged case by case, so such a distribution blocks the
   deploy whatever feature the advisory concerns.
precedent.why: The normative definition expressly excludes withdrawn OSV entries, so an affected-version entry marked withdrawn does not constitute the known vulnerability forbidden by DEP-002.

topics.topic: Clock choice and precedence for viewer-entry rate limiting
questions: For a viewer-entry request whose rate-limit decision determines whether a session may be written, is that decision made from the operation’s wall-clock instant or from the elapsed-clock reading, and is the rate limiter an explicit exception to the wall-clock rule?

quotes:
the elapsed clock gives a duration scale: one reading per viewer-entry
  request of a clock that cannot move backwards, in seconds as a float, the same value
  `time.monotonic()` gives. It measures the viewer-entry rate-limit window of
  A25 only; a reading is kept only in that window's in-memory state, never
  written to a persisted record, never turned into an instant and never
  ordered against a persisted record.
judgement.why: The elapsed clock expressly and exclusively decides the viewer-entry rate-limit window, while the wall-clock rule governs instant comparisons rather than this monotonic duration measurement.

topics.topic: Exact boundary defining one operation for sharing a wall-clock reading
questions: What is the exact operation boundary over which one wall reading must be shared?

quotes:
An operation is what another module, the
HTTP route table or the host may call; everything else a module does is
hidden.

- **Time.** Only `system_clock` reads the host clocks (A28). An operation
  that needs the current instant takes one wall reading from it and reuses
  it; the transport guard takes the elapsed reading for the viewer-entry
  window from it. No other module reads a host clock.

An authorization check that opens its own transaction closes it before the
  caller opens one.
judgement.why: The later texts define an operation as a public module capability and treat authorization and its calling use case as separate operations, each taking and reusing its own wall reading when it needs current time.

topics.topic: Immutable container-image identity to which the vulnerability verdict is bound
questions: Which immutable image identity must the vulnerability verdict bind to, especially for multi-platform images and mutable tags?

quotes: A deploy is the start of the service from a built image.

DEP-002: the deploy step judges every distribution installed in the
built image, bound to that image's content id, against the one copy of OSV
data read in the same deploy, and starts the service only on a passing verdict about
that same image; a listed version, unreadable or unmatchable advisory
data, a verdict from an earlier deploy, or a verdict about another image
does not start it
[witness: verification:dependency_release_gate_client_portal].
judgement.divergence: One implementation binds the verdict to an immutable platform-image digest and refuses a changed tag target; another binds it to a tag, index digest, or build label and starts different platform content, which the deployment operator and users observe.
judgement.why: The refusal rule depends on image identity, but `content id` is not defined for mutable tags or multi-platform image structures.

witness.initial: A mutable tag identifies image A when checked and later identifies image B with different installed distributions.
events: The release gate checks image A through the tag and records a passing verdict under its chosen content identity.
The tag is moved to image B.
The deployment process attempts to start the tag.
outcomes: Digest binding detects that image B was not checked and refuses to start it.
Tag or build-label binding treats the verdict as applicable and starts image B.
witness.observer: The deployment operator and users of image B
basis: A deploy is the start of the service from a built image.

An image in
which a distribution has a known vulnerability is not deployed; only an
image that passes the check is, whether the fix was a pin changed through
the Factory route (rule 2) or a rebuild that resolved a fixed library
under the same pins.

topics.topic: Required verification that every current-time comparison reuses the unchanged wall reading
questions: What Required test demonstrates, for every operation and every current-time comparison it performs, that the comparison uses the unchanged single wall reading rather than a derived, cached, or otherwise altered value?

quotes:
CLK-002: the clock source is the only reader of the host's wall and
elapsed clocks; an operation takes one wall reading, and that instant
decides every current-time comparison it makes and every portal-owned
timestamp it writes (the audit writer's reading of `occurred_at` aside);

CLK-002: a source check that no module other than the clock source
imports the `time` module or calls `now`, `utcnow` or `today` of
`datetime` or `date`, under any name, and that only the A25 viewer-entry
rate limiter calls the elapsed reading, passing its value to no store,
no audit and no `datetime` or `timedelta`; a test per operation that
reads the wall clock, with a counting wall-clock source, that the
operation takes exactly one wall reading and the audit writer one per
appended record, and that an expiry equal to that reading is refused
while the timestamps it writes equal that reading; and a viewer-entry
test with a counting clock source that one request takes exactly one
elapsed reading and that the window decision at its boundary follows
that reading.
judgement.divergence: One verifier checks only read counts and one equality boundary and accepts another comparison made against an adjusted value; another verifies every current-time comparison against the unchanged reading and rejects it, while the affected caller sees acceptance or refusal at that boundary.
judgement.why: The Required tests do not state how every current-time comparison in each operation is enumerated and proven to use the unchanged single reading.

witness.initial: An operation has two persisted-expiry comparisons, and the implementation compares the second expiry with the single reading plus an adjustment.
events: The operation receives wall time T from the counting clock source.
The first expiry comparison uses T and satisfies the stated equality-boundary assertion.
The second comparison uses T plus an adjustment without another clock read.
outcomes: A test covering only the read count and first equality boundary passes the implementation.
A test requiring every comparison to use exactly T fails the implementation.
witness.observer: The release verifier and a caller at the second expiry boundary
basis:
An expiry is valid strictly before its instant: a
session, credential or token is usable while `now < expires_at` and expired
from `now = expires_at` on (Factory code `application/authorization_guard.py`,
`application/service_identity.py`).

How many readings an operation takes and which instant it reuses stay the
rules above.

topics.topic: Verification that the production clock backend performs one fresh, unchanged host read
questions: What required test or source check shows that the production clock source itself performs one fresh host read and returns it unchanged, rather than caching or adjusting it?

quotes:
the wall clock gives the instant: the current UTC time as an offset-naive
  datetime, one reading per operation for its own timestamps, the same value
  `datetime.utcnow()` gives (no cache, no local time, no second reading by
  the operation, no arithmetic in the clock source; an operation derives
  an expiry by adding its TTL to the instant it read); the audit writer's reading of an appended
  record's `occurred_at` is the one further reading (the exception above);

CLK-002: a source check that no module other than the clock source
imports the `time` module or calls `now`, `utcnow` or `today` of
`datetime` or `date`, under any name, and that only the A25 viewer-entry
rate limiter calls the elapsed reading, passing its value to no store,
no audit and no `datetime` or `timedelta`; a test per operation that
reads the wall clock, with a counting wall-clock source, that the
operation takes exactly one wall reading and the audit writer one per
appended record, and that an expiry equal to that reading is refused
while the timestamps it writes equal that reading; and a viewer-entry
test with a counting clock source that one request takes exactly one
elapsed reading and that the window decision at its boundary follows
that reading.
judgement.divergence: One verifier substitutes a counting source only at operation boundaries and accepts a production backend that caches or adjusts host time; another verifies a fresh unchanged host read per backend call and rejects it, and repository readers observe stale or shifted timestamps.
judgement.why: The Required tests verify consumers of the source but do not say what demonstrates the production backend's no-cache, no-arithmetic, fresh-read obligations.

witness.initial: The production clock source caches its first host-wall reading and returns it unchanged to later operations.
events: A first operation calls the production source and stores its returned timestamp.
A second operation calls the source once and stores the cached timestamp.
The operation-level counting and equality assertions run with a supplied test source.
outcomes: The tests pass because each operation called its source once and stored the returned value.
A production-backend freshness test fails because the second call did not perform a fresh host read.
witness.observer: The release verifier and readers of the persisted timestamps
basis:
the wall clock gives the instant: the current UTC time as an offset-naive
  datetime, one reading per operation for its own timestamps, the same value
  `datetime.utcnow()` gives (no cache, no local time, no second reading by
  the operation, no arithmetic in the clock source; an operation derives
  an expiry by adding its TTL to the instant it read); the audit writer's reading of an appended
  record's `occurred_at` is the one further reading (the exception above);

topics.topic: Which operations must take exactly one wall-clock reading
questions: Must every portal operation, including read-only operations and operations that neither compare current time nor write timestamps, take exactly one wall reading, or only operations that need current time?

judgement.why: This is the same question as P2 about whether operations that do not need current time take a wall reading, and the deciding later-state passage has not changed.

precedent.topic: Whether clock-independent operations take one wall-clock reading or none
quotes:
- **Time.** Only `system_clock` reads the host clocks (A28). An operation
  that needs the current instant takes one wall reading from it and reuses
  it; the transport guard takes the elapsed reading for the viewer-entry
  window from it. No other module reads a host clock.
precedent.why: The later module rule limits the wall reading to an operation that needs the current instant, so an operation with no timestamp or current-time comparison takes none.
